title: Diabetes and feet: preventing wounds and acting early
intro: Diabetes can damage the nerves and blood supply in the feet. A blister may be painless yet become a serious wound, so pain is not a reliable guide to safety. Daily checks, suitable footwear, regular professional assessment and quick action on new changes work together. A previous ulcer means ongoing prevention is particularly important, even after healing.

sections.heading: Know your personal risk
paragraphs: Loss of protective sensation makes pressure, rubbing and heat harder to notice. Reduced circulation slows healing, while changes in foot shape concentrate pressure on small areas. Ask your diabetes team to assess sensation, circulation, skin, nails, footwear and any previous ulcer or amputation. A complete foot assessment is usually needed at least yearly, with more frequent specialist follow-up for higher risk. The team should explain your risk level and provide a clear contact route for new problems. Glucose, blood pressure and cholesterol management and support to stop smoking help protect health, but good numbers do not make a new foot wound harmless.

sections.heading: Build a daily inspection into an ordinary routine
paragraphs: In good light, inspect the tops, soles, heels and spaces between toes for blisters, cracks, broken skin, blood, swelling or changes in colour and warmth. A mirror or help from a trusted person can make this possible if reaching or seeing the feet is difficult. Check inside shoes for grit, damaged lining or other objects before putting them on. Wash gently in warm, not hot, water, checking temperature safely rather than with a numb foot; avoid soaking. Dry carefully between toes. Moisturise dry skin on the feet but not between the toes. Ask the team to demonstrate care that fits your mobility, vision and living situation.

sections.heading: Prevent pressure, burns and accidental cuts
paragraphs: Wear well-fitting protective shoes and clean socks, including indoors; walking barefoot or only in socks can allow injury. Shoes need room for the toes without slipping or rubbing. Check feet after briefly wearing new shoes and stop using a pair that causes a mark or blister. Deformity or previous ulcers may require prescribed footwear or insoles and regular fit checks. Do not use hot water bottles, heating pads, sharp blades, acid corn treatments or medicated corn plasters on the feet. Arrange professional care for calluses, thick or ingrowing nails, or if you cannot see, feel or reach safely. Do not dig at a nail corner or cut away hard skin yourself.

sections.heading: New changes need prompt assessment, even without pain
paragraphs: Contact the diabetes or foot team the same day about a new wound, blister, discharge, persistent red mark or an unusually hot, red or swollen foot. Do not wait for the next routine appointment or for pain. A hot swollen foot may be infection or acute Charcot damage to bones and joints; it can occur with intact skin. Avoid putting weight on a suspected Charcot foot while arranging urgent assessment, and ask how to move safely. A suddenly cold, pale or blue foot, black tissue, rapidly spreading infection, fever with a wound, severe illness or confusion needs emergency care. Redness can be less obvious on darker skin: warmth, swelling and colour change also matter.

sections.heading: A wound needs a treatment plan, not just a dressing
paragraphs: If skin is broken, protect it with a clean dressing, reduce pressure and seek advice; do not burst blisters or apply harsh chemicals or home remedies. Specialist care may include assessing blood supply, relieving pressure with an appropriate device, wound cleaning and treatment of infection when present. Antibiotics are not a substitute for pressure relief or circulation assessment and are not routinely needed for an uninfected ulcer. Ask exactly how much weight you may bear, who changes dressings and when the wound will be reviewed. Agree what to do outside clinic hours. Early care can prevent serious harm, but prevention should continue after healing because recurrence remains possible.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a painless warning
examples.text: Dan notices a blood mark on his sock after trying new shoes, but feels no pain. He stops wearing the shoes, checks the foot, protects the broken skin and contacts his foot team that day. Lack of pain does not reassure him that it is safe to keep walking on it.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: making checks accessible
examples.text: Ana cannot bend far enough to see her heels. With her agreement, her daughter helps with a daily check and they keep the urgent foot-service contact beside her medicines. Her clinician also arranges professional nail care and an appropriate review schedule.

questions: What is my foot risk, and how often do I need professional checks?
Which shoes and daily care are safe for my sensation and circulation?
Who should I contact today or outside normal hours if a new change appears?
